articles.title: LIV Golf begins laying off employees while restructuring without Saudi funding
articles.summary: LIV Golf has informed employees their jobs will end next week as the league begins life without Saudi funding.
articles.body:
LIV Golf has informed employees their jobs will end next week as the league begins life without Saudi funding, downsizing operations as it pursues an agreement with a lead investor to reshape the league for next year.

It was not clear how many or what percentage of employees are being laid off. LIV ended its fifth season last week outside Indianapolis, one week earlier than expected.

The staff reduction was not a surprise. LIV Golf learned in April the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia would end financial backing after this season. LIV in July filed a notice under the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act that indicated layoffs were likely.

There also was hope that several employees could be hired back depending on LIV securing its agreement with the lead investor and how the new league — LIV 2.0 — might look.

"The funding commitment announced by PIF earlier this year will reach its conclusion. As a result, we are scaling back operations as we transition to the next chapter of LIV Golf and work toward making LIV 2.0 a reality," LIV said in a statement Wednesday.

"This week, we informed many of our colleagues that their employment under LIV 1.0 will end in the first week of September. We are grateful to our employees for their hard work and dedication in building LIV Golf, and we remain committed to supporting those affected through this transition."

CEO Scott O'Neil announced earlier this month that he had come to terms with a lead investor, which multiple reports have indicated was BC Partners, and they were hopeful of finalizing the deal in September.

LIV Golf had its shortest season since the year it launched in 2022, losing events in New Orleans and the team championship in Michigan, with the team title merged into the Indiana event.

Still to be determined are the futures of its biggest names, starting with Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau. Rahm still is under contract while DeChambeau started the year negotiating for a renewal. That was before Saudi Arabia pulled the plug on the funding when the Iran war led PIF to reshape its investment priorities.

O'Neil has not ruled out filing for bankruptcy as part of the restructuring. LIV already faces two lawsuits for not paying vendors for services.

Tyrrell Hatton, a four-time Ryder Cup player from England who joined LIV in 2024 with Rahm's team, entered the British Masters this week once he learned the team championship in Michigan had been canceled.

He said Wednesday he has "multiple years" on his contract with LIV. Hatton plans to play five of the next seven weeks on the European tour beginning with the British Masters, which starts the qualifying period for the Ryder Cup for Team Europe.

He said he expects LIV Golf to be playing in 2027.

"I know they have worked really hard to getting funding stuff in place. So I know it's full steam ahead on that front," Hatton said. He also said he has continued to play the European tour and "I don't see why that should change for me in the future."

O'Neil has pitched a 10-tournament schedule for LIV, half of them overseas and half in the United States. Key to that plan is making sure his players can compete anywhere, though his mantra of "Complete, Not Compete" didn't sit well with tours that lost players to big signing bonuses.

The PGA Tour has banned LIV players for at least one year dating to their last LIV appearance. An exception was made for five-time major champion Brooks Koepka, who ended his contract with LIV at the end of 2025 and returned to the PGA Tour under stiff financial penalty.

O'Neil said last week in Indiana the first stage of LIV required big investments.

"This next chapter requires something quite different — commercial discipline," he said. "I wasn't here in the early days, but at least reputationally, it was a bit more free-spending than it will be in the future. We've taken a real disciplined look at the cost side of the business."

images.caption: LIV Golf begins laying off employees while restructuring without Saudi funding

articles.title: LPGA Tour announces plans for an event in Hong Kong beginning next year
articles.summary: The LPGA Tour and presenting sponsor Moomoo announced plans Wednesday for an event in Hong Kong beginning next year.
articles.body:
NORTON, Mass. — The LPGA Tour and presenting sponsor Moomoo announced plans Wednesday for an event in Hong Kong beginning next year.

The tour said the Futu Ladies World Championship is scheduled for March 4-7 at The Clearwater Bay Golf & Country Club. A field of 78 players is set to compete for a $3.4 million purse, the highest of any LPGA Tour event in Asia.

The LPGA is back in New England for the third FM Championship at TPC Boston from Aug. 27-30 and features a field of 144 players.
tags: The Clearwater Bay Golf & Country Club

articles.title: Good Good Golf withdraw from title sponsoring PGA Tour event after controversial ad promoting new Callaway driver
articles.summary: Content creators Good Good Golf pull out of title sponsoring PGA Tour event in November, saying "we recognise that we have work to do as an organisation"; Brand apologised for publishing a video for a Callaway driver last week that has been accused of portraying violence against women
articles.body:
The video published last week by the popular content creators was subsequently deleted after widespread criticism that it portrayed violence against women.

The video showed a man shoving a woman who was reaching for his new Callaway driver to the ground, before warning her not to touch the club as she lay on the ground.

Good Good Golf apologised in a social media statement and Callaway Golf admitted 'mistakes were made' over their handling of the incident.

The company had been due to title sponsor a new PGA Tour event in Austin in November but have now pulled out of doing so.

In a statement on Thursday, Good Good Golf said: "After thoughtful discussion with the PGA Tour and careful reflection, we have decided to step away as sponsor of the tour event in Austin this fall.

"We recognise that we have work to do as an organisation, and our focus right now is on our team, our culture and ensuring we learn from this situation.

"We are grateful for our relationship with the PGA Tour and appreciate their partnership over the years. We remain committed to earning back trust, and we hope to work together again in the future."

The PGA Tour issued its own statement and said it agreed with the decision.

"The PGA Tour has been informed of Good Good Golf's decision to step away as sponsor of the event in Austin, Texas, this fall," read the statement.

"We agree with their decision to use this time to focus on their organization and the work ahead.

"The PGA Tour believes in golf's ability to bring people together and create a welcoming environment for all.

"The tournament will continue as scheduled from November 12-15, 2026, and we will provide an update on sponsorship plans at a later date."

Earlier on Thursday, Callaway confirmed it had ended its relationship with Good Good with immediate effect.

The golf equipment manufacturer said it would donate $1m (£736,000) to "support organisations working to prevent violence against women, provide resources to survivors, and advance education and awareness efforts".

They also said they had "significantly strengthened our approval procedures to help ensure this does not happen again".

"Over the last several days, we have reflected deeply on the hurt and disappointment caused by the video we reposted," read the Callaway statement.

"We heard from individuals who shared personal experiences related to violence against women, and their stories were powerful reminders that this issue touches the lives of far too many people.

"Unequivocally, violence against women is unacceptable and should never be trivialised, normalised, or used as entertainment."

Good Good Golf was launched as a YouTube channel in 2020 and now is among the largest content creators in the sport.

"We posted a video to our channels that ultimately depicted actions that are not aligned with our values as a brand," read the Good Good apology on X on Saturday. "We have since taken that content down, and sincerely apologise.

"Good Good has always stood for making the game of golf more inclusive to all, and we will continue to ensure that is our mission moving forward".

images.caption: Image: The PGA Tour agrees with Good Good Golf's 'decision to use this time to focus on their organisation and the work ahead'

articles.title: Chase for $10 million: Min Woo Lee uses YouTube, new irons to charge to Tour Championship lead
articles.summary: It's been a slog of a year for Lee, but after Round 1, he's two shots clear of the field in the season finale.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — A note for all the kids out there who are surely reading this article: Don't let your parents limit your YouTube time! And if they try, tell them they're keeping you from being a professional golfer!

Coming into the PGA Tour's FedEx Cup playoffs, Min Woo Lee was struggling. Ranked 31st in the world, 21st in the field of 30, Lee hadn't won on Tour since March 2025. Three days ago, he posted a message on Instagram: "Average 2 weeks. Onto the Season finale, Down In Atlanta."

You could feel the resignation radiating from the post.

"It was probably the saddest I've been on the golf course, which is not good," he said Thursday afternoon. "We're really lucky to be out here and play some good golf to get into the playoffs. It just felt so hard."

For his first three holes on Thursday at East Lake Golf Club, Lee was the definition of average once again. But after a trio of pars, Lee caught fire, and cooked with eight birdies over the final 15 holes. He finished the day with a 62 that left him at -8, two strokes clear of the field but two strokes short of Zach Johnson's 60 in 2007.

"This week was a brand-new week, and we obviously play from scratch and everyone plays from the same score," Lee said. "Being out there, I thought, Why not give it a good crack and have a good attitude? That was probably a thing that I had to work on over the last two weeks."

The new attitude helped, and so did a late change to his irons, combined with a review of YouTube highlights of past performances at East Lake. This is Lee's first time on the property, and he needed to familiarize himself with the layout. "I know the course has changed a tiny bit," he said. "I know the guys that have played really well here."

Many, though not all, of those guys struggled on Thursday. Viktor Hovland, 2023 champion, is one of three sitting two strokes behind Lee, along with Chris Gotterup and Collin Morikawa. Three-time champion Rory McIlroy is at -2, mired deep in the field at T20. Last year's champion, Tommy Fleetwood, sits at -4, tied for 8th, while Scottie Scheffler is lurking at -5 after closing with two birdies.

"This week, you just have to perform and get the best out of yourself for one week," Hovland said. "I feel like when I can put myself in that mindset, I tend to get a lot out of my game."

This year's tournament is a winner-take-all affair, as opposed to previous years when players received a stroke advantage based on where they'd finished during the season. That means players deep in the field — like, say, Lee — don't need to be quite as aggressive to mount a charge up the leaderboard.

"I think you treat it like any other tournament," Morikawa said. "You're not playing more aggressive just because you only have four rounds to end the season. You're not going to do anything stupid."

The Tour Championship, with a $40 million purse and a $10 million first prize, continues through Sunday and wraps up the 2026 PGA Tour season.

articles.title: TOUR Championship Leaderboard 2026 Review of Top Scorecards, Player Stats on Day 1
articles.summary: Min Woo Lee holds the lead after 18 holes at the Tour Championship.
articles.body:
Min Woo Lee holds the lead after 18 holes at the Tour Championship.

The Australian owns a two-stroke edge over Viktor Hovland, Collin Morikawa and Chris Gotterup at East Lake Golf Club.

Scottie Scheffler, who recorded the most FedEx Cup points this season, is lurking three shots back of Lee in a tie for fifth.

Whichever golfer finishes with the lowest score after four rounds comes away with the FedEx Cup. Twenty-nine golfers are left in the field after J.J. Spaun's Thursday withdrawal.

The full leaderboard can be found here on PGATour.com.

Min Woo Lee carded an eight-under 62 to take control of the tournament after 18 holes.

Lee split four birdies on the front nine and four more on the back nine. He did not drop a shot and rolled in 10 pars.

Six of Lee's eight birdies occurred on consecutive holes. He finished the round with a birdie on the par-five 18th hole.

The stellar round is a bit surprising because Lee finished in a tie for 55th and a tie for 47th in the first two rounds of the FedEx Cup Playoffs.

If he keeps this up for three more rounds, he could outpace the field and end up as an unlikely winner.

Scottie Scheffler's birdies on the 17th and 18th holes moved him into a tie for fifth.

Scheffler rolled in birdies on the third, sixth and 12th holes prior to his consecutive birdies to end the round.

Outside of that, Scheffler produced 13 pars throughout his opening round.

Scheffler likely feels the most pressure in the field this week because he finished with such a wide advantage in the FedEx Cup standings.

FedEx Cup points don't mean anything now with the tournament being a straight-up stroke-play event.

Scheffler turned in a solid start to potentially finish off his season-long reign in the standings come Sunday.

articles.title: Tour Championship: Min Woo Lee leads with Tommy Fleetwood in contention
articles.summary: Defending champion Tommy Fleetwood shoots a four-under 66 to put himself in contention at the Tour Championship at East Lake in Atlanta.
articles.body:
8 MW Lee (Aus); -6 V Hovland (Nor), C Morikawa (US), C Gotterup (US); -5 R Gerard (US), A Bhatia (US), L Aberg (Swe), S Scheffler (US)

Selected others: -4 T Fleetwood (Eng), M Fitzpatrick (Eng), R Fox (NZ); -3 R MacIntyre (Sco), W Clark (US); -2 J Rose (Eng), A Fitzpatrick (Eng), R McIlroy (NI)

Defending champion Tommy Fleetwood shot a four-under 66 to put himself in contention, four strokes off first-round leader Min Woo Lee at the Tour Championship in Atlanta.

However, Northern Ireland's Rory McIlroy endured a mixed start in his bid to win a record-extending fourth Fedex Cup, bogeying two of the first four holes before fighting back on the back nine to sign for a 68.

Lee carded a bogey-free 62 to set the pace at eight under as he equalled his best round on the PGA Tour in its season-ending event at East Lake.

Australia's Lee is two strokes clear of Norway's Viktor Hovland, who triumphed in 2023, and American duo Collin Morikawa and Chris Gotterup.

It was a fine display from Lee, who was second from last in the BMW Championship a week ago and found himself without a partner for most of the day, with JJ Spaun withdrawing through injury after four holes.

"It was a little strange at first, just like looking for a playing partner and you're just there by yourself," said Lee.

"It was more just maintaining speeds and not rushing because I would just catch the group in front and wait. So I had to just slow down a little bit. It worked out."

Ominously, world number one Scottie Scheffler ended his round with a birdie on the 18th to sit at five under, with England's Matt Fitzpatrick in the mix at four under after also making a birdie four on the concluding hole.

Scotland's Robert MacIntyre is at three under, with the highlight of his day arriving on the sixth hole when he rolled in a putt from over 30 feet for an eagle.

England's Justin Rose and Alex Fitzpatrick both signed for rounds of 68 on a day when none of the 29 players in the field to complete the round went over par.

The winner on Sunday will take home the Fedex Cup and a $10m (£7.4m) prize.

There will be live text coverage of the final round on the BBC Sport website and app from 18:00 BST.

articles.title: Tour Championship: Min Woo Lee leads FedExCup finale with Scottie Scheffler chasing after Rory McIlroy's mixed start
articles.summary: Scottie Scheffler is three off the early lead and Rory McIlroy is six behind at East Lake; Min Woo Lee holds a two-shot advantage at the Tour Championship after a low-scoring opening round; watch throughout the week live on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
Lee carded eight birdies in a bogey-free 62 at East Lake Golf Club, where preferred lies were used due to overnight rain and none of the 29 players who completed the round failed to break par.

The Australian holds a two-shot advantage over Chris Gotterup, Viktor Hovland and Collin Morikawa, as world No 1 Scottie Scheffler produced a birdie-birdie finish to his opening-round 65 to get within three of the lead.

Ludvig Åberg, Akshay Bhatia and Ryan Gerard are alongside Scheffler on five under, while defending champion Tommy Fleetwood is a further shot adrift in the group containing compatriot Matt Fitzpatrick and Open winner Ryan Fox.

Last week's BMW Championship winner Wyndham Clark is five behind after a three-under 67, as McIlroy sits tied-20th after beginning his bid for a record-extending fourth FedExCup title by mixing five birdies with three bogeys in an eventful 68.

Lee posted back-to-back birdies from the fourth and was left undisrupted by playing the remainder of the round on his own, following playing partner JJ Spaun's withdrawal on the sixth hole due to a shoulder injury.

The 28-year-old kept trading top spot with Hovland, playing two groups ahead, with Lee closing out a bogey-free front nine by holing a 20-foot birdie at the eighth and picking up another shot at the ninth.

Lee posted back-to-back birdies from the 12th and added another from close range at the 16th, moving him two ahead when Hovland ended his blemish-free day by carding a three-putt bogey from 25 feet at the 17th.

Hovland responded by getting up and down from the greenside bunker to birdie the par-five last, setting the clubhouse target at six under, before Lee matched his closing birdie to restore his two-shot cushion and equal the lowest round of his PGA Tour career.

"It was a little strange at first, just like looking for a playing partner and you're just there by yourself," Lee admitted. "It was more just maintaining speeds and not rushing. I had to just slow down a little bit, but it worked out."

Morikawa responded from an opening-hole bogey to register seven birdies and pull level with Hovland, while Gotterup birdied three of his last five holes to make it a three-way tie for second.

Åberg produced a three-birdie finish to get to five under alongside Bhatia and Gerard, with Scheffler completing the quartet tied-fifth having holed a 10-foot birdie at the last to start with a 65 or lower for the fourth time in five seasons.

"Outside of the first hole, I wasn't really battling for par very much," Scheffler said. "That's always good around this place. Every time you miss a fairway out here, you're going to be struggling for par. Gave myself some opportunities and was able to make a couple birdies there at the end."

McIlroy briefly sat bottom of the leaderboard after failing to get up and down from the sand to save par at the first and holing from eight feet to scramble a bogey at the fourth, with the world No 2 finding a birdie at the sixth but missing an opportunity from four feet for another at the ninth.

He posted two birdies in three holes to start his back nine and rebounded from a clumsy bogey at the 14th to hole a six-foot birdie at the par-three next, with McIlroy adding another at the 17th but heading into the second round with only five players below him on the leaderboard.

articles.title: FM Championship: Lottie Woad makes strong start in Boston on LPGA Tour amid final tournaments before Solheim Cup
articles.summary: England's Lottie Woad four off the early pace at the LPGA's FM Championship, while South Africa's Casandra Alexander shoots course record on day one at KPMG Women's Irish Open; final events on women's tours live on Sky Sports this week before Solheim Cup from September 11
articles.body:
England's Woad is one of 12 members of Anna Nordqvist's European team heading to the Netherlands for the September 11-13 showpiece, live on Sky Sports , and she shot a 68 at TPC Boston on Thursday to sit four shots off the pace set by Korea's Sei Young Kim.

Woad, a two-time winner on the LPGA Tour since turning professional last year, picked up all four of her birdies on the front nine to go out in 32 before parring all the remaining holes.

"I generally played a bit better on the front nine," she said.

"I hit pretty much every fairway. The rough is pretty thick out there, so you need to hit the fairways.

"Hit some pretty close shots on some holes and then did well on the par-5s getting on greens, so just kind of had tap-ins on the front nine."

"Just a couple tee shots on the back nine that missed the fairway kind of made them par holes rather than birdie holes, so just try and clean up that tomorrow."

Kim, who started on the 10th, claimed six birdies and one eagle - on the par-five seventh - in her round of 64.

Denmark's Emily Kristine Pedersen and Japan's Miyu Yamashita finished at seven-under with Somi Lee at six-under making it two Koreans in the top four.

Woad was in an eight-way tie for fifth place.

Solheim Cup team-mate Charley Hull shot a one-under 71 while world No 1 Nelly Korda, who will spearhead Angela Stanford USA's side, shot a level-par 72.

Meanwhile, European captain Nordqvist - who on Wednesday unexpectedly announced she was retiring from playing professional golf after this week - opened her swansong tournament on tour at two-over par.

Alexander hits course record at the The K Club

On day one of the Ladies European Tour's rain-hit KPMG Women's Irish Open, Casandra Alexander made a storming start by firing a course record 63 to lead the way on nine-under.

After Italy's Alessandra Fanali set the pace with a 67 at The K Club's Palmer South Course, Alexander shot four shots lower thanks to four birdies on the front nine followed by five on the back.

England's Lily May Humphreys, Czech Republic's Jana Melichova, and the Isle of Man's Ana Dawson are tied second with Fanali on five-under.

Ireland's own Leona Maguire opened with a round of 71 (-1) after three birdies and two bogeys.

Watch the KPMG Women's Irish Open and the LPGA Tour's FM Championship throughout the week live on Sky Sports. Live coverage from Ireland continues Friday from 2pm on Sky Sports+ Get latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW .

articles.title: E-bike and e-scooter battery fires cause of 18 deaths and nearly 700 injuries
articles.summary: Fatalities included people who inhaled toxic fumes from fires or became trapped inside burning homes.
articles.body:
Eighteen people have died and nearly 700 have been injured in fires caused by e-bikes and e-scooters, new data shows.

Fatalities recorded by fire and rescue services across the UK from these fires include cases where people became trapped inside burning homes, died while trying to escape from a fire out of a high window, or from inhaling toxic smoke.

More than 2,000 fires were started by e-bikes, e-scooters or their batteries between 2019 and 2025, Freedom of Information requests made by BBC Verify show.

The number of incidents has risen year-on-year and nearly half the fires started in homes or garages, the data shows.

London Fire Brigade Assistant Commissioner Pam Oparaocha told BBC Verify the service is "increasingly concerned by the significant fire risk" some of these vehicles can pose.

"From our investigations we know many of the fires we've attended have involved second-hand vehicles or the bike has been modified using parts bought online. We urge people to be extremely careful about where they buy their e-bike or e-scooter from," she added.

Footage of fires caused by e-bikes and e-scooters show how quickly the vehicles can start smoking and then apparently explode, causing blazes that spread within minutes.

An average of 153,000 new e-bikes have been added to the UK's roads each year since 2020, according to cycling industry trade body, the Bicycle Association.

The cost of a new e-bike ranges from around £400 to £4,000 in high street retailers such as Halfords or Decathlon, while second-hand vehicles and unregulated e-bike conversion kits can be found on online marketplaces for as little as £150.

Any lithium-ion battery sold in the UK for these vehicles must meet safety requirements set out by the government that ensures the batteries can be charged safely, do not overheat and are protected from damage.

The government's "Buy Safe, Be Safe" campaign states that while millions of people use these vehicles safely every day, the risk of fire can increase if they don't meet safety rules, are damaged, modified or used with an incompatible charger. It also says people should look for UKCE or CE product safety marks when buying an e-bike or e-scooter.

The number of fires caused by e-bike and e-scooter batteries has increased dramatically from 32 in 2019 to 605 in 2025, according to the data gathered by BBC Verify.

The highest numbers of incidents were recorded by fire and rescue services in urban areas, with 793 recorded in London over the seven year period, 128 in Manchester, 93 in West Yorkshire, 74 in Merseyside and 73 in Avon.

Lithium-ion batteries are useful because they store a huge amount of energy in a small space, Dr Simon Jones at the University of Warwick, who led research into the safety of e-bikes and e-scooter batteries for the Office for Product and Safety Standards, told BBC Verify.

"However, if these batteries are faulty, over-charged or damaged, the stored energy may be released rapidly in the form of flame jets and burning projectiles," he said.

"If this occurs in the home this is likely to result in a fast spreading fire that can engulf a room in seconds and block escape routes, trapping people inside. These fires also release toxic fumes from the batteries that pose a serious risk to health."

Jahmell Campbell, 24, from London, said when his e-scooter caught fire "it was the loudest explosion I'd ever heard".

He was at his grandmother's home in Hither Green in March last year when the vehicle burst into flames by the front door.

"The only way out was through the window, so I jumped straight out," he said.

Jahmell said he ran to the back of the building, and realised his grandmother was trapped. He made his father throw a blanket down for her to escape.

"My dad had to throw her out the window and we had to catch her," he said.

His grandmother suffered minor injuries after hitting a windowsill on the way down.

"Somehow we all made it out with our lives intact, which honestly shouldn't have happened," he added.

Six fire engines attended to fight the blaze. The flat, where his grandmother had lived for over 20 years, was destroyed.

Several coroners have warned about the dangers posed by these batteries and have issued at least five Prevention of Future Deaths reports since 2023, with recommendations to improve public safety.

Among those cases was eight-year-old Luke Albiston-O'Donnell from Birkenhead , who died after inhaling toxic fumes from a house fire caused by an e-bike battery on charge in 2024. Following an inquest, coroner Anita Bhardwaj warned: "The general public do not appreciate the life-threatening risks involved with having lithium-ion batteries, from electronic bikes in this case, stored in domestic properties."

Mohsin Janjua, a 28-year-old man from Bradford, died in similar circumstances in 2023 . Later investigations found a "catastrophic failure" of the battery in an e-bike conversion kit purchased online from China was "more likely than not" responsible for the fire.

Other coroners linked fatalities to e-bikes and e-scooters that did not conform to UK safety standards.

Steve Garidis from the Bicycle Association said retailers have invested in developing safe and legal e-bikes but this can be "undermined by illegal and unsafe products often sold through online marketplaces to unsuspecting consumers".

The Bicycle Association and the Association of Cycle Traders run an "E-Bike Positive" scheme to help consumers identify distributors, retailers and manufacturers that have met current safety standards.

They have also called on the government to crack down on the sale of unsafe e-bikes through online marketplaces and tackle the demand for cheap e-bikes and scooters driven by the gig economy.

A government spokesperson said: "Unsafe e-bike and e-scooter batteries can pose a serious fire risk, which is why we are taking action to protect consumers.

"This includes strengthening the responsibilities of online marketplaces to better protect consumers, working with local authorities to identify and remove unsafe products from sale, and helping people make informed choices through our 'Buy Safe, Be Safe' campaign."

BBC Verify sent Freedom of Information requests to all 49 fire and rescue services in the UK, asking for data on fires where the source of ignition was recorded as an e-bike or e-scooter, including associated batteries. Forty-one provided comparable responses. Greater Manchester and West Sussex were unable to provide data on casualties, fatalities, and the number of fires that happened in dwellings.

While some fire and rescue services log e-bikes and e-scooters as a distinct category, others provided data by performing a text search for "e-bike", "e-scooter" and similar keywords. While this provides a reasonable estimate of incidents, some reports may not have been picked up in this search if e-bikes or e-scooters were not mentioned directly.

articles.title: Callaway ditches golf brand Good Good over sexist video backlash
articles.summary: Golf club manufacturer Callaway ends its partnership with content creator Good Good with immediate effect and donates $1m to women's charity after promoting advert that shows a woman being pushed over.
articles.body:
Golf club manufacturer Callaway has ended its partnership with content creator Good Good with immediate effect following backlash over a video which showed a woman being pushed to the ground after reaching for a club.

American golf brand Good Good has one of the most popular sport YouTube channels with 2.13m subscribers and had created and published the advert for Callaway last week.

But the video drew widespread criticism and was accused of making light of violence against women, and both companies removed the advert and issued apologies.

Good Good, who Callaway has worked with since 2023, has also stepped away from its sponsorship of a PGA Tour event in Austin, Texas in November.

On Thursday, Callaway, in a statement on X, , external conceded its content review process "was not comprehensive enough", adding that it had "listened and reflected deeply on the hurt and disappointment caused by the video we reposted".

The manufacturer said it was also donating $1m (£735,725) to organisations working to prevent violence against women and support victims.

"We heard from individuals who shared personal experiences related to violence against women, and their stories were powerful reminders that this issue touches the lives of far too many people," Callaway's statement read.

"Unequivocally, violence against women is unacceptable and should never be trivialised, normalised, or used as entertainment."

Callaway said they have taken "appropriate internal corrective actions" to help ensure this does not happen again.

The advert showed Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark rushing over to Alexis Miestowski - a professional golfer and regular content creator for Good Good - and pushing her to the ground before shouting: "Do not touch my new driver."

The brand, which has become one of the largest content creators in golf, launched its YouTube channel 2020.

Regular clips include men and women competing in various golf challenges, while Good Good also creates made-for-TV shows as well as adverts for golf clothing and other merchandise.

After pulling out as sponsors of the PGA Tour tournament, Good Good chief executive officer Matt Kendrick said they "remain committed to earning back" the tour's trust.

"We recognise that we have work to do as an organisation, and our focus right now is on our team, our culture and ensuring we learn from this situation." Kendrick added in a statement.

articles.title: Gary Woodland isn’t just playing for himself anymore. His newfound purpose in life is way bigger than that
articles.summary: If there’s a more uplifting comeback story anywhere in the sports world right now than Gary Woodland, it’s hard to imagine.
articles.body: If there’s a more uplifting comeback story anywhere in the sports world right now, I’d like to know about it. Simply put, American golfer Gary Woodland is beyond inspiring. He’s courageous, resilient and the very that fact he’s even playing in this week’s season-ending Tour Championship less than three years after undergoing surgery to remove a tumor on his brain is truly remarkable. “My wife Gabby’s my rock. She’s the one that reminds me why in tough times I’m here, what I’m fighting for. The only dream I’ve ever had is to be a professional athlete. I owe it to my childhood self to fight every day. There’s a lot of days where I don’t want to do it. There’s a lot of days I don’t want to fight, but my wife reminds me why I am,” Woodland told CNN Sports a day before his first round at this week’s Tour Championship at East Lake Golf Club in Atlanta. “It’s a tribute to my family who sacrificed so much and gave everything for me to go out and live my dreams. I owe it to everyone else, I’m not just playing for myself,” he added. The 42-year-old – who’s playing in the season-ending tournament for the first time in seven years – revealed earlier this year that he also suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder following that surgery in September 2023. It means Woodland feels ill at ease when faced with large crowds and he has a security detail out on the course to help reassure him that he’s safe and protected while playing. “My good days now are 10s. Like when I have a good day, I think I’m more appreciative. I have better perspective. My bad days are still 1s. So, I struggle sometimes because it’s a massive drop now from 10 to 1. So, when I get off, it feels like the end of the world,” Woodland said. Woodland says everything he’s been through in recent times has led to fresh perspectives on life and a now-burning desire to help and inspire other people who are enduring their own hardships. “Before all this started, I thought it was about me. This is way bigger than me now. I owe it to them, and I owe it to everyone else that is struggling,” the 2019 US Open champion said. “I had a kid in Memphis who flew over from New Zealand, who’s 11 years old and has an inoperable brain tumor, and he wanted to meet me. Wednesday through Sunday, he walked every hole with me. I owe it to him. This is a lot bigger than myself now; I realize that. So, when I’m struggling, I fight for them.” The Kansas native has been in impressive form this year. He finished tied for fourth at the recent BMW Championship to break into the FedEx Cup standings’ top 30 and his highly emotional victory at the Texas Children’s Houston Open was his first win on the PGA Tour since his brain surgery. In fact, it was also his first win since that breakthrough career major triumph at Pebble Beach seven years ago, and it came just days after he’d shared news of his PTSD diagnosis. But don’t think for one moment that Woodland is at East Lake just to make up the numbers, far from it. His hunger for a sixth tour title and continued success remains very front and center for him. “I have the ability to get up and fight every day, and I’m going to do that. I have a lot of fight left in me. I believe I have a big career left ahead of me, and I’m not going to let this thing win. At the end of the day, I truly believe I can beat this thing. It’s not easy, but I’ll keep fighting every day to do it.” To say Gary Woodland has the full respect and admiration of his fellow professionals would be an understatement and there would surely not be a more beloved winner in golf if the American could go on win the coveted FedEx Cup this week. “I think he’s been amazing in how he’s been open about his journey with us all. He doesn’t have to do that for sure. For him to have a great year, it’s one of those inspirational stories that I’m sure touches so many people and also has an impact on a lot of people as well and their individual journeys,” said Tommy Fleetwood, the 2025 FedEx Cup champion. “Gary’s done amazing this year. He’s an amazing golfer, but he’s had to deal with a lot of things. It’s just shown what you can do in certain situations. Very proud of him,” the Englishman added. By breaking into the Tour Championship’s elite 30-man field this week, Woodland has a chance to win the season-ending title, which would be a remarkable achievement in its own right and especially so for a golfer who now has a totally newfound purpose in life. “At the end of the day, I want to make this world a better place. If my story or my journey or me talking about the struggles I face every day, if that helps somebody else, that’s what it’s all about,” he said. “I don’t want to be remembered as being a great golfer. I want to be remembered as a great person. Hopefully, my struggles – my struggles suck. There’s no other way to put it. I have a lot of days that suck, but if that helps somebody else, then that’s going to help me too.”

Woodland speaks during a news conference at the Tour Championship in Atlanta.
Woodland plays his shot on the third tee during the first round of the Tour Championship golf tournament.

articles.title: Golders Green: Four admit arson attack on Jewish ambulances
articles.summary: Four vehicles run by a charity were set alight in Golders Green, north-west London, causing explosions in March.
articles.body:
Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing £1m of damage in north-west London.

Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, and Saif Ali, both aged 18, pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.

The attack, which took place in the early hours of 23 March, saw four vehicles operated by the charity Hatzola set alight in Golders Green.

Prosecutors had said they believed the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.

The court heard three of the men set fire to the fully stocked ambulances, while a fourth had waited in a nearby car.

After the ambulances were set alight, gas canisters exploded inside the vehicles.

As well as destroying each of the £250,000 vehicles, the fire damaged four electrical charging stations and cables costing approximately £5,000 each.

Leo Seelig, prosecuting, told the court that the Crown Prosecution Service would be arguing that the four men should be sentenced on the basis that the arson attack was related to terrorism.

Mrs Justice Cheema Grubb said she would not rule on the question of terrorism at this stage - with defence counsel arguing that there was no evidence for such a connection.

The judge said that the four would be sentenced following the outcome a trial of a fifth man, Subhan Ahmed, who has denied assisting an offender.

Iqbal and Khan, of Leyton, Atshatshi, of Dagenham, and Ali, of Walthamstow, were remanded into custody.

Run by volunteers, Hatzola has served the north London community of Golders Green, which has a large Jewish population, since 1979.

Hatzola, the Hebrew word for save or rescue, is a large non-profit, Jewish-led organisation that provides a free emergency medical response and transportation to hospitals regardless of faith by volunteer medics.

Community Security Trust, a charity working to protect British Jews from terrorism and antisemitism, welcomed the pleas and said the four's actions "caused immense shock and distress across the Jewish community".

"This was an appalling antisemitic act against a volunteer ambulance service providing emergency medical assistance to people of all backgrounds across north London, simply because those ambulances belonged to a Jewish charity," a spokesperson added.

When the group are sentenced - which is expected to be in spring next year - prosecutors will allege that the incident was connected to terrorism. Lawyers for the men have told the court today that none of them are involved in terrorism.

The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026.

They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack.

That position has been further confirmed in their minds by the FBI's investigation of and allegations against an Iranian-Iraqi man facing trial in Manhattan for orchestrating a series of attacks against Jewish communities across Europe

US court papers allege that Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a commander of an Iraqi militia, was linked to attacks in London, including the destruction of Jewish charity ambulances.

In May al-Saadi was arrested in Turkey and extradited to the US, with the US Department of Justice alleging he had a role in planning more than a dozen terrorist attacks in North America and Europe .

Publicly available court papers list a series of incidents across Europe that the FBI says he is linked to. In many cases the attacks on Jewish community interests were claimed online by a shadowy group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, or the The Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand.

The US court papers say that the social media account for the group posted claims saying it was behind the ambulance attacks - and that al-Saadi had himself posted social media propaganda videos of the attack.

"On or about March 23, 2026, at approximately 1:45 a.m., three masked individuals carried out an arson attack on four Hatzalah Ambulances in London, United Kingdom," reads the indictment before the US court.

"That same day, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya posted on Telegram a propaganda video in which it claimed responsibility for the attack. On or about March 25, 2026, AL-SAADI posted on social media propaganda videos of the attack."

The Department of Justice also alleges that Al-Saadi posted another propaganda videos relating to an attempted arson attack on Finchley Road Synagogue in north London in April.

US lawyers for Al-Saadi have said previously that he is a political prisoner.

articles.title: Good Good Golf CEO criticizes Callaway for dropping partnership, says it was part of 'coordinated media blitz'
articles.summary: Good Good Golf is going on the offensive after losing its partnership with Callaway.
articles.body:
After being put on the defensive following backlash to a controversial ad, one prominent member of Good Good Golf has had enough. Co-Founder and CEO Matt Kendrick ripped Callaway on Friday after the company decided to drop its partnership with Good Good.

In a post on X, Kendrick called out Callaway for approving the ad in the first place. He said he believed Callaway dropped Good Good as part of a "coordinated media blitz" and then attempted to absolve itself of wrongdoing by making a $1 million donation.

"Interesting that @CallawayGolf asks us to make an ad then approves it then asks us to take the fall then drops us in a coordinated media blitz and covers it up by giving a million dollars away thinking everyone will be ok with it. 30 for 39 [sic] will be legendary."

Good Good found itself embroiled in controversy after releasing an ad last Thursday in which one of its other co-founders pushed a woman to the ground because she was going to touch a driver.

That ad was removed a day later, with Good Good offering an apology. Eventually, Callaway — which partnered with Good Good and approved the ad — also apologized.

The situation then escalated , with PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp calling out the company. That same day, it was reported Good Good merchandise was being pulled off store shelves.

On Thursday — a week after the ad was released — Callaway decided to end its partnership with Good Good. In a statement, Callaway announced it would give $1 million to charities aimed at preventing domestic violence. That decision came hours after Garrett Clark — the Good Good co-founder who appeared in the ad — tried to explain how the ad got released.

After his tweet Friday, Kendrick took some time to respond to fan comments on X. He admitted Good Good "made a terrible ad," and thanked those who were still supporting the company.

Kendrick also apparently had additional responses that have since been deleted , one of which reportedly implied Good Good planned to file a lawsuit , per the New York Post.

Kendrick, however, attempted to clarify his stance to Front Office Sports later Friday. After saying he did not see the ad before it aired, Kendrick said the members of the marketing team who approved it are no longer with Good Good. He also said Good Good has no intention to sue Callaway.

articles.title: Good Good Golf doesn't deserve to be canceled for their dumb ad in collaboration with Callaway
articles.summary: Good Good Golf faces cancel culture as retailers and the PGA Tour pull support over a Callaway ad, while Callaway itself faces no repercussions.
articles.body: Cancel culture is making a comeback, unfortunately. In case you missed it, Good Good Golf has been dragged by the golf establishment for an advertisement they posted in collaboration with Callaway golf, which promoted the Quantum Max Driver with Good Good branding. The ad features many of Good Good's top personalities, including co-founder Garrett Clark, who is seen shoving a woman before she's able to get a hold of the driver in his bag. He stands over her as she lays on the ground and tells her not to touch his driver. Reading this makes it sound bad, and watching it is "cringe," as Clark stated, while apologizing in a lengthy Instagram post following the backlash. The advertisement was done and presented in poor taste and the public didn't receive it well. Even though it was meant to take inspiration from the hit horror movie "Obsession," as Clark stated in his instagram video, where a character becomes obsessed with another due to a magic spell, causing them to be insanely and violently overprotective, it was not perceived that way. Many viewers missed the point and it fell flat, to say the least. But, what has been done in the aftermath since the deleted post, is what is unjust and concerning to me. NFL PUTS 'INSPIRE CHANGE' AND 'CHOOSE LOVE' ON FIELDS BUT NOT SO AGGRESSIVE ABOUT ITS DOMESTIC ABUSE ISSUES This whole situation has turned into a way for companies to virtue signal about domestic violence and supporting women, though most, if not all of these companies have done nothing to protect women and girls as their sports and spaces have been invaded by males over the years. Clark, in a 9-minute long video said neither him, nor the company, support or meant to insinuate any form of domestic violence. It was clearly a skit, but retail companies and even the PGA Tour are actively cancelling the popular YouTube golf brand, making them the fall guy for an ad that Callaway is just as responsible for, in my opinion. YOUTUBE GOLFER GRANT HORVAT IS SELLING KIDS GOLF CLUBS WITH AN ALARMINGLY HIGH PRICE TAG Golf Galaxy, Dick's Sporting Goods, Target, and the PGA Superstore have pulled Good Good products from their shelves and online. Golf Channel cancelled the latest season of the reality show in collaboration with Good Good, "Big Break." Good Good announced Thursday the cancelation of their title sponsorship for the PGA Tour event, the Good Good Championship in Texas saying, "After thoughtful discussion with the PGA Tour and careful reflection, we have decided to step away as sponsor of the Tour event in Austin this Fall." Callaway also ended their partnership with the popular golf brand stating, "we have listened and reflected deeply on the hurt and disappointment caused by the video we reposted. We heard from individuals who shared personal experiences related to violence against women, and their stories were powerful reminders that this issue touches the lives of far too many people. Unequivocally, violence against women is unacceptable and should never be trivialized, normalized, or used as entertainment." Yes, violence and mistreatment of women should be called out and women and girls should be protected, but these decisions and statements are just pure, unadulterated corporate virtue signaling. MARY CAIN'S BOOK AND NIKE'S TRANS-ATHLETE STUDY REVEAL THE SAME PATTERN OF CORPORATE HYPOCRISY Here's the worst part: Has Callaway's merch been pulled from stores? Nope. Has Callaway dealt with any reprecussions from the PGA Tour? Nope. That is exactly what Good Good Golf CEO, Matt Kendrick called out early this morning in a post on X stating, "Interesting that @CallawayGolf asks us to make an ad then approves it then asks us to take the fall then drops us in a coordinated media blitz and covers it up by giving a million dollars away thinking everyone will be ok with it." Bingo. In other words, Good Good is the bad guy, and Callaway gets to virtue signal their way into receiving no backlash from the golf establishment and media because they're donating $1 million "to support organizations working to prevent violence against women, provide resources to survivors, and advance education and awareness efforts." Good grief. Get off your high horse, Callaway. This is clear and obvious cancel culture. PEREZ HILTON JOINS 'TOMI LAHREN IS FEARLESS' AND DECLARES CANCEL CULTURE IS NOW A SPORT Cancel culture is an unjustified public shaming and social ostracism for a perceived wrong, mostly due to something liberals consider not politically correct under their ridiculous societal standards. It's not an actual wrong, worthy of relentless public shaming and corporate canceling. When I told people publicly to avoid shopping and supporting Bud Light, Target, Ulta and others promoting transgenderism through kids clothing, "tuck-friendly" swimwear, a man pretending to be a woman telling women how to be women (Dylan Mulvaney), that is not cancel culture. That's an objective moral wrong. Companies promoting body mutilation through "gender affirming care", gender fluidity, and more nonsense, is worth boycotting. FROM COLIN KAEPERNICK TO DYLAN MULVANEY, NIKE'S DECADE OF LEFT-WING ACTIVISM HAS FINALLY CAUGHT UP TO IT The Bud Light boycott was the most successful boycott in recent history after they partnered with Mulvaney to celebrate "one year of womanhood." It was a justified boycott. Anyone comparing Bud Light to this poorly-acted, dumb advertisement, which was obviously presented in poor taste, is being dishonest. Cancel culture was Twitter banning and suspending accounts like The Babylon Bee, myself, Charlie Kirk, and many others years ago, for calling former Assistant Secretary for Health under the Biden administration, Rachel Levine and swimmer Lia Thomas, men. DAN GAINOR: WE GOT TWITTER/X AS A PLATFORM 20 YEARS AGO AND GLOBAL CENSORS STILL HATE AND FEAR IT Cancel Culture is Fanatics firing from hosting their live shows in 2021 because I went to the gym without a mask in Arizona, the day the Governor dropped the mask mandate. What is being done to Good Good is cancel culture. It’s wrong. Clark never actually shoved that woman, as he stated on Instagram. It was acting. Yes, poor acting and a very bad idea. I've stated online that I have no idea why they thought this way a good idea, especially in a culture ready and willing to overreact, but it was in no way a promotion or endorsement of domestic violence. NIKE REMOVES RUNNING AD IN BOSTON FOR 'PACE SHAMING' I can relate to this in a real way because I was an actor in a video for my Christian college's chapel program, where I played a version of the old Terry Tate: Office Linebacker Reebok commercial, where he tackled men and men throughout the office. I "tackled" and "shoved" men and women in the video. I even stood over a female chapel card monitor yelling at her for accepting a blank chapel attendance card from a student. It was clearly satire. It was a dumb, yet fun video. No women were harmed. No women were outraged. Thousands laughed when it was shown at a semester-end chapel. No one was canceled or was called to be canceled. There have been many advertisements over the years with men tackling or shoving women. Betty White got trucked in a Snickers commercial playing football. In an early 2000s commercial, Michelob Ultra portrayed a woman getting viciously tackled in a football game at a park. There was a clear understanding of satire and acting. It wasn't real. It wasn't a prescription for abusing women. More than anything, there's a clear double standard at play with the way Callaway is being treated by the PGA Tour, Golf Channel, and retailers. Callaway saw this dumb advertisement in collaboration with Good Good Golf, signed off on it, published it, and they are going through the situation unscathed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP No, I'm not calling for Callaway to be canceled. Both should have just said the ad was dumb, apologized for how it was received, taking accountability for a lack of clear messaging, saying that it was a spin-off of Obessesion, and move on. Instead, Good Good is faced with their products no longer in major retailers, pushed out of their title sponsorship for a PGA Tour event, and a public corporate shaming that is one of the worst in history. All because the PGA Tour and corporations want to make an example out of a group, so they can look morally superior. It's shameful.
